cards.definition: The part of a cell that contains genetic information and controls the cell.
The part of a cell that makes protein.
The part of a cell that releases energy.
The bigger of the two numbers 1x10⁻⁵ and 1x10⁻⁶ — a larger negative exponent means a smaller number.
The type of microscope with the lowest magnification.
The clarity of a microscope image — how much detail can be seen.
The amount an object has been made bigger by a microscope.
Primitive cells that have no nucleus, e.g. bacteria.
More advanced cells that contain a nucleus, e.g. animal and plant cells.
A microscope not used in school because it is too expensive and requires too much training — but gives much higher magnification than a light microscope.
The process in which cells become specialised for a particular function.
Undifferentiated cells that have not yet become specialised.
Where stem cells are stored for use in medical research.
The type of tumour that can spread to other parts of the body.
The type of tumour that remains encapsulated and does not spread.
The process in which cells make copies of themselves to produce body cells.
The process in which sex cells (gametes) are created.
The process of releasing energy from glucose using oxygen.
The process of releasing energy from glucose without using oxygen; also used to make beer and bread.
The anaerobic process used by yeast to produce alcohol and carbon dioxide, used in making beer and bread.
Carbon dioxide and water are the two reactants needed for photosynthesis.
Glucose and oxygen are the two products of photosynthesis.
The process by which particles move from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction — it takes in energy from light.
One of the four substances glucose can be converted into in plants; used for storage of energy.
One of the four substances glucose can be converted into; used to make cell walls.
One of the four substances glucose can be converted into; used for storage of energy in plants.
One of the four substances glucose can be converted into; used for growth and repair of cells.
The test for starch — iodine solution turns from orange to blue-black in the presence of starch.
The organelle inside plant cells that carries out photosynthesis, containing the pigment chlorophyll.
The green chemical inside chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
The small holes in the bottom of a leaf through which gases enter and leave.
The cells on either side of a stoma that control whether it opens or closes.
The top layer of cells in a leaf, packed with chloroplasts for maximum photosynthesis.
How fast photosynthesis is happening in a plant at any given moment.
The rate of photosynthesis can be measured by counting bubbles of oxygen produced or measuring the volume of oxygen.
The movement of water through a plant from roots to leaves, where it evaporates.
The tube that carries water and minerals up through a plant from roots to leaves.
The tube that carries sugary water (glucose solution) around a plant.
A factor such as light intensity, CO₂ concentration or temperature that limits the rate of photosynthesis.
The movement of water molecules from a high water concentration to a low water concentration through a partially permeable membrane.
During diffusion, particles move from high concentration to low concentration — down the concentration gradient.
The movement of particles against the concentration gradient, which requires energy.
The system that transports substances such as oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide around the body.
The system that exchanges gases (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out) in the body.
The system that moves and breaks down nutrients through the body for absorption.
Biological catalysts that speed up digestion and other chemical reactions in the body.
The test for glucose — Benedict's solution turns from blue to orange/red in the presence of glucose.
The test for protein — Biuret solution turns from blue to purple/lilac in the presence of protein.
Iodine solution turns from orange to blue-black in the presence of starch.
Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart to the body.
Blood vessels that carry blood back into the heart from the body.
The two top chambers of the heart that receive blood.
The two bottom chambers of the heart that pump blood out.
Blood that has had its oxygen removed by the body's cells; found on the right side of the heart.
The liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances including carbon dioxide, glucose and urea.
A small tube inserted into a blocked blood vessel to keep it open.
The chemical in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.
The smallest blood vessels where substances are exchanged between blood and body cells.
Structures in the heart and veins that prevent blood from flowing backwards.
A disease that cannot be passed on to other people, e.g. cancer, diabetes.
A disease that can be passed on to other people, e.g. flu, HIV.
A cancerous tumour that can spread to other parts of the body.
A non-cancerous tumour that remains in one place and does not spread.
Single-celled microorganisms that can cause diseases such as gonorrhoea and food poisoning.
A non-living pathogen that causes diseases such as HIV and influenza.
A type of microorganism responsible for diseases such as athlete's foot.
A type of microorganism responsible for diseases such as malaria.
A virus that attacks the immune system; spread through bodily fluids.
A communicable disease caused by a protozoan pathogen, spread by mosquitoes.
Physical defences that stop pathogens entering the body, including skin, scabs, tears, nose hairs and mucus.
The cells of the immune system that fight off infections.
Proteins produced by white blood cells that target and destroy specific pathogens.
Chemicals produced by white blood cells that neutralise toxins released by pathogens.
A poison released by a microbe that harms the body.
A microorganism that has infected the body and causes disease.
The state of being able to defend against reinfection by a specific pathogen.
A preparation containing dead or weakened pathogens that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies.
Drugs used to kill bacterial infections; they do not work against viruses.
The gold standard in drug trials — neither the patient nor the doctor knows who receives the drug or the placebo.
The process of controlling the body's internal environment to maintain stable conditions.
Three internal conditions that must be controlled are temperature, water levels and blood glucose.
A response that is fast and specific to a particular stimulus.
A response that is slower and affects the whole body via chemicals in the blood.
Made up of the brain and spinal cord; coordinates the body's responses.
The part of the nervous system that detects changes in the environment (stimuli).
The two types of effector are muscles (which contract) and glands (which secrete hormones).
The neurone that sends signals from the CNS to effectors.
The neurone that sends signals from receptors to the CNS.
The neurone that connects the sensory neurone to the motor neurone in reflex actions.
The junction between two neurones where signals are passed using chemicals.
The chemical that moves across a synapse to pass a signal from one neurone to the next.
The organ that releases hormones into the bloodstream.
The chemical form in which glucose is stored in the liver and muscles in humans.
The two hormones involved in controlling blood glucose levels.
The condition that prevents people from controlling their blood glucose levels.
The hormone that stimulates the release of an egg from the ovary.
The hormone that causes the uterus lining to thicken in preparation for pregnancy.
The hormone that stimulates an egg to mature in the ovary.
A treatment for fertility problems where eggs are fertilised outside the body.
The organelle that controls the cell and contains genetic information in the form of chromosomes.
A thread-like package of DNA found in the nucleus of a cell.
The type of cell division that makes identical body cells.
The type of cell division that makes sex cells (gametes) with half the normal number of chromosomes.
The first cell before cell division takes place.
The cells produced as a result of cell division.
The number of chromosomes found in a human sex cell (gamete).
The number of chromosomes found in a human body cell.
The name for sperm and egg cells — the sex cells used in reproduction.
The cell formed through fertilisation when a sperm and egg cell fuse.
Characteristics caused by genes passed on from parents, e.g. eye colour.
Characteristics caused by the world around us rather than by genes.
The process of the development of new species over many generations through natural selection.
Random changes to DNA that can produce new characteristics.
The specific characteristics that help an organism to survive in its environment.
The continued existence of organisms that are best suited to their environment.
The scientist who developed the theory of evolution by natural selection.
The remains or evidence of the existence of dead organisms preserved in rock.
What happens to most organisms when they die — broken down by microorganisms.
An example of a bacterium that has evolved to be resistant to antibiotics through natural selection.
The process by which humans choose organisms to breed based upon their desirable characteristics.
The characteristics that humans want an organism to have when selectively breeding.
The differences between organisms caused by differences in their DNA.
Crops that have been genetically modified to be toxic to pests.
The manipulation of an organism's genes to give it new characteristics.
A circular strand of DNA found in bacteria, used as a vector in genetic engineering.
A small section of DNA that codes for a specific characteristic or protein.
Chains of amino acids coded for by genes; all enzymes are proteins.
The grouping of organisms based on their shared characteristics.
When there are none of a species left alive anywhere on Earth.
The variety of all the different species on Earth or within a particular ecosystem.
A community of living organisms and the non-living environment they interact with.
The natural home of an organism — the place where it lives.
The number of organisms of a particular species living in a given area.
The mutual reliance between two or more groups of organisms on each other.
Physical (non-living) factors such as temperature and light intensity that affect population size.
Living factors such as predation and disease that affect population size.
The place or role of an organism within its ecosystem.
The process by which an organism becomes better suited to its environment over time.
An organism that thrives in physically extreme conditions such as very high temperatures or acidity.
The process by which carbon moves through the environment between living organisms and the atmosphere.
The process by which plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to make glucose.
The process by which organisms release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere when releasing energy.
The process by which energy and carbon dioxide are released through burning fuels.
Organisms such as bacteria and fungi that break down dead living material, releasing carbon.
Fuels made from dead organisms over millions of years, e.g. coal, oil and natural gas.
The two main gases responsible for global warming are carbon dioxide and methane.
The process of cutting down large areas of trees, reducing CO₂ absorption and biodiversity.
The process of dealing with pollution in the air, water and on land.
Organisms that show whether an area is polluted by their presence or absence.
